about: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures): written from each verse, its word meanings, Monier-Williams and Apte and Śaṅkara's reading, starting from the owner's drafts, then reviewed, copy-audited against Besant and Telang and checked again against the verse (docs/HOW-TO.md, Write our own meanings for a Sanskrit work); one piece per verse line, other readings in footnotes.

dhyana.1: Om. You who were taught to Pārtha by the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself,
woven by Vyāsa, the ancient sage, into the midst of the Mahābhārata,
who shower the nectar of non-duality, the blessed one of eighteen chapters,
O Mother, O Bhagavad Gītā, foe of worldly existence, on you I meditate again and again.
dhyana.2: Salutation to you, O Vyāsa of vast intellect,
whose eyes are long as the petals of a full-blown lotus,
you by whom a lamp filled with the oil of the Mahābhārata,
a lamp made of knowledge, was lit.
dhyana.3: To him who is the wish-granting pārijāta tree for those who take refuge in him,
who holds the goad and the cane in one hand,
to Kṛṣṇa, whose hand shows the gesture of knowledge,
who milks the nectar of the Gītā, salutation.
dhyana.4: All the Upaniṣads are the cows;
the one who milks them is Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd's son;
Pārtha is the calf; the wise man is the one who drinks;
and the milk is the great nectar of the Gītā.
dhyana.5: The son of Vasudeva, the divine one,
the crusher of Kaṃsa and Cāṇūra,
to Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, I bow.
dhyana.6: Bhīṣma and Droṇa its banks, Jayadratha its water, Gāndhārī its blue lotus,
Śalya its crocodile, Kṛpa its current, Karṇa its surging tide,
Aśvatthāman and Vikarṇa its dreadful sea-monsters, Duryodhana its whirlpool:
that river of battle the Pāṇḍavas indeed crossed, with Keśava as their boatman.
dhyana.7: The spotless lotus that is the word of Parāśara's son, rich with the fragrance of the Gītā's meaning,
its filaments the many tales, opened by the telling of the story of Hari,
which the good in the world, as bees, drink again and again with joy, day after day:
may this lotus of the Mahābhārata, destroyer of the taint of the Kali age, be for the highest good.
dhyana.8: the lame it makes cross a mountain:
I bow to him whose grace it is,
dhyana.9: To him whom Brahmā, Varuṇa, Indra, Rudra and the Maruts praise with divine hymns,
whom the singers of the Sāma sing with the Vedas, with their auxiliary sciences, their pada and krama recitations and the Upaniṣads,
whom yogīs see with a mind settled in meditation and absorbed in him,
whose end the hosts of gods and asuras do not know: to that God, salutation.
1.1: On the field of dharma, of what is right, at Kurukṣetra, gathered together and eager to fight,
my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu, what did they do, O Sañjaya?
1.2: Seeing the Pāṇḍava army arrayed for battle,
King Duryodhana then went up to the teacher Droṇa and spoke these words.
1.3: Look, O teacher, at this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
drawn up by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
1.4: Here are heroes, great archers, equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna:
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior;
1.5: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valiant king of Kāśī;
Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, the best of men;
1.6: Yudhāmanyu the bold and Uttamaujas the valiant;
Subhadrā's son and Draupadī's sons, every one of them a great chariot-warrior.
1.7: Now take note, O best of the twice-born, of those who are distinguished on our side,
the leaders of my army; I name them to you so that you know them.
1.8: You yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, victorious in battle;
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta;
1.9: and many other heroes who for my sake have given up all thought of their own lives,
bearing many kinds of weapons, all of them skilled in war.
1.10: That army of ours, guarded by Bhīṣma, is insufficient,
while this army of theirs, guarded by Bhīma, is sufficient.
1.11: So, standing in your assigned places at all the entrances of the array,
all of you, every one, must indeed guard Bhīṣma above all, on every side.
1.12: Bringing joy to Duryodhana, the grandsire, the eldest of the Kurus,
the mighty Bhīṣma gave a loud lion's roar and blew his conch.
1.13: Then conches and kettledrums, tabors, drums and cow-horns
were all struck up at once, and that sound became a tumult.
1.14: Then, with white horses yoked to the great chariot in which they stood,
Mādhava and Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, blew their divine conches too.
1.15: Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta;
Vṛkodara, Bhīma of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
1.16: King Yudhiṣṭhira, Kuntī's son, blew the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka.
1.17: The king of Kāśī, the supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and Sātyaki the unconquered,
1.18: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, all of them, O lord of the earth,
and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā blew their conches, each his own.
1.19: That uproar tore apart the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
a tumult that made the sky and the earth resound.
1.20: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in position, Arjuna, whose banner bore the monkey,
the son of Pāṇḍu, raised his bow as the loosing of weapons was about to begin,
1.21: and then spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa, O lord of the earth.
O Acyuta, halt my chariot between the two armies,
1.22: while I look over these who stand here eager to fight,
and see with whom I have to fight in this undertaking of war.
1.23: Let me look at those who are ready to fight, who have gathered here
wishing to do in battle what pleases the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
1.24: Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, Arjuna, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa
halted the finest of chariots between the two armies
1.25: facing Bhīṣma and Droṇa and every ruler of the earth,
and said: O Pārtha, see these Kurus gathered here.
1.26: There Pārtha saw, standing, elders of his father's rank and grandfathers,
teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends too,
1.27: fathers-in-law and well-wishers as well, in both the armies.
Looking closely at all those kinsmen standing there, the son of Kuntī,
1.28: filled with deep compassion, spoke this in despair.
Seeing these my own people, O Kṛṣṇa, come here eager to fight,
1.29: my limbs fail me and my mouth dries up;
a trembling comes over my body, and my hair bristles.
1.30: The bow Gāṇḍīva is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning everywhere;
I cannot stand steady, and my mind seems to whirl.
1.31: And I see adverse omens, O Keśava,
and I see no good in killing my own people in battle.
1.32: I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
What use to us is a kingdom, O Govinda, or enjoyments, or life?
1.33: Those for whose sake we desired kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures,
these very ones stand here in battle, having renounced their lives and riches:
1.34: teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers,
uncles on the mother's side, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other kinsmen.
1.35: These I do not wish to kill, O Madhusūdana, even if they kill me;
not even for the kingdom of the three worlds; how much less for the sake of the earth?
1.36: What joy could we have, O Janārdana, from slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
Sin alone would take hold of us if we killed these aggressors.
1.37: Therefore it is not fit for us to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen.
For, having killed our own people, how could we be happy, O Mādhava?
1.38: Even though these men, their minds overpowered by greed, do not see
the evil that comes of destroying a family, or the sin in treachery to friends,
1.39: why should we not know enough to turn back from this sin,
we who clearly see the evil that comes of destroying a family, O Janārdana?
1.40: When a family is destroyed, its age-old family dharmas perish;
when dharma is lost, adharma, unrighteousness, overpowers the whole family as well.
1.41: When adharma prevails, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupted;
and when the women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, a mixing of varṇas, the social orders, arises.
1.42: This mixing leads both the family-destroyers and the family itself to hell;
for their forefathers fall, deprived of the rites of offering piṇḍa, the rice-balls, and water.
1.43: Through these misdeeds of the family-destroyers, which bring about a mixing of varṇas,
the dharmas of caste and the everlasting family dharmas are uprooted.
1.44: For men whose family dharmas have been uprooted, O Janārdana,
a dwelling in hell is certain: so we have heard.
1.45: Alas, what a great sin we have resolved to commit,
in that, through greed for the pleasures of a kingdom, we are ready to kill our own people!
1.46: If, while I am unresisting and unarmed, with weapons in their hands
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were to kill me in battle, that would be the better for me.
1.47: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of the chariot;
he cast aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.
1.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the first chapter, named Arjunaviṣādayoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despondency.
2.1: To him, thus filled with compassion, his eyes troubled and filled with tears,
sinking in despair, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
2.2: From where has this dejection come upon you at this perilous hour?
It is the way of the ignoble, O Arjuna; it does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
2.3: Do not give way to unmanliness, O Pārtha; this is not fitting for you.
Cast off this petty weakness of heart and stand up, O scorcher of foes.
2.4: How, O Madhusūdana, shall I on the battlefield, against Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
fight back with arrows? They are both worthy of worship, O slayer of enemies.
2.5: Rather than slay these noble-souled gurus,
it is better to live even on alms here in this world.
But if I slay my gurus, though they seek their own gain,
I would enjoy, here in this very world, pleasures smeared with blood.
2.6: And we do not know which would be better for us,
whether we should conquer, or they should conquer us.
Those very men, after killing whom we would not wish to live,
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, stand arrayed before us.
2.7: My nature is struck down by the fault of poorness of spirit;
with my mind confused about dharma, I ask you:
tell me what would be certainly good.
I am your disciple; teach me, for I have taken refuge in you.
2.8: For I do not see what could drive away from me
the grief that dries up my senses,
even if I were to gain on earth a prosperous kingdom without a rival,
or even lordship over the gods.
2.9: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, O king, scorcher of foes, Guḍākeśa, Arjuna,
told Govinda that he would not fight, and fell silent.
2.10: O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling,
spoke these words to him as he sat despairing between the two armies.
2.11: You have grieved for those who are not to be grieved for, and yet you speak words of wisdom.
The wise grieve neither for those whose breath has gone nor for those whose breath has not gone.
2.12: Never at any time was I not, nor you, nor these rulers of men;
nor is it that hereafter we shall all cease to be.
2.13: Just as the embodied one passes in this body through childhood, youth and old age,
so it comes to another body; the wise one is not deluded by this.
2.14: But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, give cold and heat, pleasure and pain;
they arrive and depart, and are impermanent: bear them, O Bhārata.
2.15: For the person whom these do not trouble, O best of men,
who is the same in pain and pleasure, the wise one, is fit for immortality.
2.16: Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no ceasing to be.
The final truth of both of these has been seen by those who see things as they are.
2.17: But know this: that by which all this is pervaded is indestructible.
No one is able to destroy this imperishable one.
2.18: It is said that these bodies of the eternal embodied one have an end;
the embodied one is indestructible and immeasurable. Therefore fight, O Bhārata.
2.19: He who takes this one for a slayer, and he who thinks it slain:
neither of them understands; it neither slays nor is slain.
2.20: It is never born, nor does it ever die;
nor is it that, having been, it will not be again.
It is unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient;
it is not slain when the body is slain.
2.21: He who knows this one to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and imperishable,
how, O Pārtha, can that person cause anyone to be slain, and whom can he slay?
2.22: Just as, casting off worn-out clothes,
a man puts on other, new ones,
the embodied one passes into other, new ones.
2.23: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it;
water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.
2.24: It cannot be cut, it cannot be burnt, it cannot be wetted, and it cannot be dried either.
It is eternal, all-pervading, firm, immovable and everlasting.
2.25: It is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable and unchanging.
Therefore, knowing it to be so, you should not grieve.
2.26: And if you think of it as constantly being born or constantly dying,
even then, O mighty-armed one, you should not grieve like this.
2.27: For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died;
therefore you should not grieve over a thing that cannot be avoided.
2.28: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning and manifest in their middle, O Bhārata,
and unmanifest again in their end; what lament can there be over this?
2.29: One sees this Self as a wonder;
likewise another speaks of it as a wonder;
and another hears of it as a wonder;
and even having heard of it, no one knows it.
2.30: This embodied one, in the body of every being, can never be slain, O Bhārata;
therefore you should not grieve for any being.
2.31: Moreover, considering your own dharma, your sacred duty, you should not waver;
for there is nothing better for a kṣatriya, a man of the warrior order, than a war in keeping with dharma.
2.32: Come about of its own accord, this war is an open door to heaven;
fortunate are the kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who meet with such a war.
2.33: But if you will not fight this battle that is in keeping with dharma,
then, having cast away your own dharma and your good name, you will incur sin.
2.34: Moreover, people will speak of your disgrace, a disgrace that will never pass;
and for one who has been held in honour, disgrace is worse than death.
2.35: The great chariot-warriors will take it that you turned back from battle out of fear;
and among those who held you in high esteem, you will be made light of.
2.36: Your enemies will say many things that ought not to be said,
belittling your strength; what could be more painful than that?
2.37: Slain, you will gain heaven; or victorious, you will enjoy the earth;
therefore rise, O son of Kuntī, resolved to fight.
2.38: Holding pleasure and pain alike, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
then make ready for battle; so you will not incur sin.
2.39: This understanding has been set forth to you as it bears on Sāṅkhya, the discernment of the Self; now hear it as it bears on yoga, the discipline of action,
endowed with which understanding, O Pārtha, you will cast off the bondage of action.
2.40: On this path no effort once begun is lost, and no contrary result arises;
even a little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
2.41: On this path, O joy of the Kurus, the resolute understanding is one;
but the understandings of the irresolute have many branches and no end.
2.42: The unwise proclaim this flowery speech,
delighting in the words of the Veda, O Pārtha, and saying there is nothing else;
2.43: their nature is desire, and heaven is their highest goal; their speech offers birth as the fruit of action
and is full of many particular rites for gaining enjoyment and power.
2.44: Those who cling to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by that speech —
in their mind (samādhi) no resolute understanding is formed.
2.45: The Vedas deal with the three guṇas, the qualities of nature; rise above the three guṇas, O Arjuna:
be free from the pairs of opposites, ever abiding in sattva, the quality of purity, free from the care of gaining and keeping, and self-possessed.
2.46: Whatever purpose a well serves is all served where water floods on every side;
just so, whatever purpose all the Vedas serve is all gained by the brāhmaṇa who knows the truth.
2.47: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits;
do not become the cause of the fruit of action, and let there be no attachment in you to inaction.
2.48: Established in yoga, do your actions, O Dhanañjaya, giving up attachment,
and being even in success and failure; this evenness is called yoga.
2.49: For action is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, O Dhanañjaya;
seek refuge in understanding; pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit.
2.50: One endowed with understanding casts off, here in this world, both good and evil deeds;
therefore devote yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
2.51: For the wise, endowed with understanding, give up the fruit born of action,
and freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state where there is no sorrow.
2.52: When your understanding has crossed beyond the mire of delusion,
then you will grow indifferent to what is yet to be heard and to what has been heard.
2.53: When your understanding, now distracted by the many scriptures it has heard, stands unwavering,
immovable in the Self (samādhi), then you will attain yoga.
2.54: How is one of steady wisdom, who abides in samādhi, to be described, O Keśava?
How does one of steady mind speak, how does he sit, how does he move?
2.55: When one wholly gives up all the desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha,
and is content in the Self alone, by the Self, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
2.56: He whose mind is not shaken in sorrows, whose craving for pleasures has gone,
from whom attachment, fear and anger have departed — such a sage is called one of steady mind.
2.57: He who is without attachment anywhere, who, meeting with this or that, good or bad,
neither rejoices nor hates — his wisdom is firmly established.
2.58: And when, as a tortoise draws in its limbs on every side, he draws in
his senses from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established.
2.59: The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who does not feed on them,
all but the relish for them; even the relish of this one turns away when he has seen the Supreme.
2.60: For, O son of Kuntī, even of a wise man who is striving,
the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind.
2.61: Restraining them all, let him sit disciplined, intent on me;
for he whose senses are under control — his wisdom is firmly established.
2.62: When a man dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises;
from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
2.63: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory, the ruin of understanding; and from the ruin of understanding he perishes.
2.64: But one who, with senses free from attraction and aversion, moves among the objects of the senses,
senses under his own control, his mind disciplined, attains serenity.
2.65: In that serenity an end comes to all his sorrows;
for the understanding of one whose mind is serene soon becomes firmly settled.
2.66: One whose mind is not disciplined has no understanding, nor has such a man contemplation;
one without contemplation has no peace, and for one without peace, where is happiness?
2.67: For the mind that follows the senses as they roam among their objects
carries away his wisdom, as the wind carries away a boat on the water.
2.68: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are restrained in every way
from the objects of the senses — his wisdom is firmly established.
2.69: What is night for all beings, in that the self-controlled one is awake;
that in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees the truth.
2.70: Into the ocean, which is ever being filled and yet stands unmoved in its bed,
so he into whom all desires enter
attains peace, and not one who longs for the objects of desire.
2.71: The man who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing,
without possessiveness and without ego, attains peace.
2.72: This, O Pārtha, is the state of abiding in Brahman; one who reaches it is not deluded.
Abiding in it even at the hour of death, he attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
2.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the second chapter, named Sāṅkhyayoga, the yoga of Sāṅkhya.
3.1: If you hold that understanding is superior to action, O Janārdana,
why then do you urge me into this dreadful action, O Keśava?
3.2: With words that seem mixed, you seem to bewilder my understanding;
so decide on the one thing and tell me that, by which I may attain the highest good.
3.3: In this world, O sinless one, a twofold steadfastness was taught by me of old:
that of the Sāṅkhyas through jñāna-yoga, the discipline of knowledge, and that of the yogīs through karma-yoga, the discipline of action.
3.4: Not by refraining from actions does a man reach freedom from action,
nor by renunciation alone does he attain perfection.
3.5: For no one ever remains even for a moment without doing action;
for everyone is made to act, helplessly, by the guṇas, the qualities born of prakṛti, primal nature.
3.6: He who restrains the organs of action and sits recalling in his mind
the objects of the senses, deluded in himself, is called a hypocrite.
3.7: But one who reins in the senses with the mind, O Arjuna,
and, unattached, takes up karma-yoga with the organs of action, excels.
3.8: Do your prescribed action, for action is better than inaction;
without action even the upkeep of your body would not be achieved.
3.9: Apart from action done for the Lord, who is yajña, the sacrifice, this world is bound by action;
for his sake, O son of Kuntī, free from attachment, perform action well.
3.10: In the beginning, having created beings together with sacrifice, Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, said:
By this you shall multiply; let this be the cow that yields the wishes you desire.
3.11: With this nourish the gods, and let the gods nourish you;
nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.
3.12: The gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you wish for;
one who enjoys what they have given without offering to them is nothing but a thief.
3.13: The good, who eat the food left over from the sacrifice, are released from every sin;
but those sinful ones eat sin who cook for their own sake.
3.14: Beings arise from food, and food comes from rain;
rain arises from sacrifice, and sacrifice is born of action.
3.15: Know that action springs from Brahman, the Veda, and that the Veda springs from the Imperishable, the Supreme Self;
therefore the all-pervading Veda is ever established in sacrifice.
3.16: He who here does not follow the wheel thus set in motion,
living in sin and delighting in the senses, lives in vain, O Pārtha.
3.17: But the man who delights in the Self alone and is satisfied in the Self
and is content in the Self alone has nothing that he must do.
3.18: For him there is no purpose at all here in what is done, nor any in what is left undone;
nor does he depend on any among all beings for any purpose.
3.19: Therefore, unattached, always perform well the action that is your duty;
for by doing action without attachment a man attains the Supreme.
3.20: For it was through action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection;
considering lokasaṅgraha too, the holding together of the world, you ought to act.
3.21: Whatever the best among men does, other people do that very thing;
whatever he sets up as the standard, the world follows.
3.22: For me, O Pārtha, there is nothing whatever to be done in the three worlds,
nothing unattained to be attained; and yet I go on in action.
3.23: For if I were ever not to engage in action untiringly,
men would follow my path in every way, O Pārtha.
3.24: These worlds would perish if I did not do action;
I would be the cause of saṅkara, the mixing of the social orders, and would destroy these beings.
3.25: As the unwise act, attached to action, O Bhārata,
so should the wise act, unattached, seeking to hold the world together.
3.26: The wise should not cause a split in the understanding of the ignorant, who are attached to action;
rather, steadfast in yoga and doing all actions well himself, he should engage them in all actions.
3.27: All actions are in every way being done by the guṇas of prakṛti;
yet one whose mind is deluded by ego thinks that he is the doer.
3.28: But one who knows the truth of the division of guṇas and of actions, O mighty-armed one,
knowing that the guṇas act among the guṇas, is not attached.
3.29: Those deluded by the guṇas of prakṛti become attached to the actions of the guṇas;
the knower of the whole should not unsettle those dull ones of partial knowledge.
3.30: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the Self,
free from desire and from possessiveness, fight, your anguish gone.
3.31: Those people who constantly follow this teaching of mine,
full of faith and without cavilling, they too are freed from the bonds of action.
3.32: But those who cavil at this teaching of mine and do not follow it,
know them to be deluded about all knowledge, devoid of discernment, and lost.
3.33: Even one who has knowledge acts according to his own nature;
beings go the way of their nature: what will restraint do?
3.34: Attraction and aversion are fixed in the object of each sense;
one should not come under the sway of these two, for they are his foes, standing in his way.
3.35: Better is one's own dharma, one's sacred duty, though imperfect, than another's dharma well carried out;
death in one's own dharma is better; another's dharma brings fear.
3.36: Then, impelled by what does a man commit sin,
even against his will, O Vārṣṇeya, as if driven to it by force?
3.37: It is desire, it is anger, born of rajas, one of the guṇas, the qualities of nature;
it is a great devourer and greatly sinful; know it to be the enemy here in the world.
3.38: As fire is covered by smoke, and a mirror by dust,
as an embryo is enclosed in its membrane, so this knowledge is covered by that desire.
3.39: Knowledge is covered by this, the constant enemy of the wise,
which has the form of desire, O son of Kuntī, and is a fire hard to fill.
3.40: The senses, the mind and the intellect are called its dwelling place;
through these it veils knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
3.41: Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, first restraining the senses,
cast off this sinful one, the destroyer of knowledge and of its realisation.
3.42: They say the senses are superior to the body; higher than the senses is the mind;
higher than the mind is the intellect; and he who is beyond even the intellect is the Self.
3.43: Thus knowing him who is beyond the intellect, and steadying yourself by your own mind,
slay, O mighty-armed one, the enemy in the form of desire, so hard to subdue.
3.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the third chapter, named Karmayoga, the yoga of action.
4.1: I declared this imperishable yoga, this discipline, to Vivasvān, the Sun-god;
Vivasvān told it to Manu, and Manu told it to Ikṣvāku.
4.2: Thus handed down from one to the next, it was known to the royal sages;
through a long lapse of time, O scorcher of foes, that yoga has been lost here in the world.
4.3: Today I have declared to you that same ancient yoga,
since you are my devotee and my friend; for this is the highest secret.
4.4: Your birth was later, and the birth of Vivasvān earlier;
how should I understand this: that you declared it at the beginning?
4.5: Many births of mine have passed, and of yours as well, O Arjuna;
I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of foes.
4.6: Though I am unborn, my self imperishable, and though I am the lord of beings,
governing my own prakṛti, my nature, I come into being through my own māyā, my power of illusion.
4.7: Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata,
and a rise of adharma, then I bring myself forth.
4.8: To protect the good and to destroy evildoers,
and to establish dharma firmly, I come into being age after age.
4.9: He who knows my divine birth and action thus, in their truth,
does not, on leaving the body, go to birth again; he comes to me, O Arjuna.
4.10: Free from attachment, fear and anger, absorbed in me, taking refuge in me,
many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have come to my being.
4.11: In whatever way people come to me, in that same way I favour them;
men follow my path in every way, O Pārtha.
4.12: Desiring success in their actions, people here worship the gods;
for in the human world success born of action comes quickly.
4.13: The fourfold order of varṇas, the classes of society, was created by me according to the division of guṇas and actions;
though I am its maker, know me, the imperishable, to be a non-doer.
4.14: Actions do not taint me, nor do I long for the fruit of action;
he who knows me thus is not bound by actions.
4.15: Knowing this, the seekers of liberation of old also performed action;
therefore it is action that you should do, as it was done by the ancients long ago.
4.16: What is action, what is inaction: about this even the wise are bewildered.
I shall tell you of that action, knowing which you will be freed from evil.
4.17: For the nature of action has to be understood, and that of forbidden action has to be understood,
and that of inaction has to be understood: hard to fathom is the way of action.
4.18: He who sees inaction in action and action in inaction
is wise among men; he is a yogī, and the doer of all action.
4.19: He whose every undertaking is free from desires and the intentions that breed them,
whose actions are burnt in the fire of knowledge: the wise call him a paṇḍita, one truly learned.
4.20: Giving up attachment to the fruit of action, ever content, depending on nothing,
though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
4.21: Free from desire, with mind and body held in check, having given up all possessions,
doing only bodily action, he incurs no sin.
4.22: Content with whatever comes unsought, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy,
even-minded in success and failure, he is not bound even though he acts.
4.23: For one whose attachment is gone, who is free, whose mind is established in knowledge,
and who acts for the sake of sacrifice, all his action melts away.
4.24: That by which the offering is made is Brahman, the Absolute; the oblation is Brahman; by Brahman it is offered into the fire that is Brahman;
Brahman alone is to be reached by him who is absorbed in action that is Brahman.
4.25: Some yogīs devote themselves to sacrifice offered to the gods alone;
others offer sacrifice by sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman.
4.26: Some offer the senses, hearing and the rest, into the fires of restraint;
others offer the sense-objects, sound and the rest, into the fires that are the senses.
4.27: Others offer all the workings of the senses and the workings of the life-breath
into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
4.28: Likewise some offer sacrifice with material goods, some with austerity, some with yoga;
and striving ascetics of firm vows make the study of scripture and knowledge their sacrifice.
4.29: Likewise others offer the prāṇa, the outgoing breath, into the apāna, the incoming breath, and the apāna into the prāṇa;
and, intent on the control of the breath, they hold back the course of both.
4.30: Others, restricting what they eat, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths.
All these know what sacrifice is, and by sacrifice their sins have been destroyed.
4.31: Those who eat the nectar left over from sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman.
This world is not for one who offers no sacrifice; how then the other, O best of the Kurus?
4.32: Thus sacrifices of many kinds are spread out in the mouth of the Veda.
Know them all to be born of action; knowing this, you will be set free.
4.33: Better than sacrifice made of material things is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes.
All action in its entirety, O Pārtha, is contained in knowledge.
4.34: Learn that by bowing down, by searching questions and by service.
The wise, who have seen the truth, will teach you that knowledge.
4.35: Knowing it, O Pāṇḍava, you will not fall again into delusion like this,
and through it you will see all beings, none left out, within yourself and also in me.
4.36: Even if you are the worst sinner among all sinners,
you will cross over all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone.
4.37: As a kindled fire burns firewood to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge burn all actions to ashes.
4.38: For there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge.
One perfected through yoga finds it himself, in due time, within his own self.
4.39: One who has faith, who is intent on it and has mastered his senses, gains knowledge;
having gained knowledge, he soon attains supreme peace.
4.40: The ignorant, the faithless and the one whose mind is full of doubt perish;
for the doubter there is neither this world, nor the one beyond, nor happiness.
4.41: Him who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts are cut away by knowledge,
and who is self-possessed, actions do not bind, O Dhanañjaya.
4.42: Therefore, with the sword of knowledge, this doubt of your own, born of ignorance and lodged in the heart,
cut away; resort to yoga, and stand up, O Bhārata.
4.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fourth chapter, named Jñānakarmasaṃnyāsayoga, the yoga of knowledge and the renunciation of action.
5.1: O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and then again yoga.
Tell me for certain the one of these two that is the better.
5.2: Renunciation and the yoga of action both bring about the highest good;
but of the two, the yoga of action excels the renunciation of action.
5.3: He who neither hates nor desires should be known as one who is ever a renunciant;
for one who is beyond the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, is released from bondage with ease.
5.4: It is the childish, not the wise, who speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as separate.
One who is rightly established in even one of them gains the fruit of both.
5.5: The state that the followers of Sāṅkhya reach is reached by the followers of Yoga as well.
He who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one sees truly.
5.6: But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga reaches Brahman before long.
5.7: One who is disciplined in yoga, pure in mind, master of his body and conqueror of his senses,
whose self has become the self of all beings, is not tainted even while he acts.
5.8: The disciplined one who knows the truth should think: I do nothing at all,
while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
5.9: speaking, letting go, taking hold, even opening and closing the eyes,
holding firmly that it is the senses that move among the objects of the senses.
5.10: Whoever places his actions in Brahman, gives up attachment and so acts
is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.
5.11: With the body, the mind and the intellect, and even with the senses alone,
yogīs act, giving up attachment, for the purification of the mind.
5.12: The disciplined one, giving up the fruit of action, attains lasting peace;
the undisciplined one, attached to the fruit through the prompting of desire, is bound.
5.13: Renouncing all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells at ease
in the city of nine gates, the body, neither acting at all nor causing action.
5.14: The master creates neither the doership nor the actions of the world,
nor the joining of action with its fruit; it is nature that is at work.
5.15: The all-pervading one takes on no one's sin, nor anyone's good deed either.
Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, beings are deluded.
5.16: But in those in whom that ignorance has been destroyed by the knowledge of the Self,
that knowledge, like the sun, reveals the Supreme.
5.17: Their intellect set on That, their self being That, steadfast in That, with That as their highest goal,
their sins shaken off by knowledge, they go where there is no return.
5.18: On a brāhmaṇa rich in learning and humility, on a cow, on an elephant,
on a dog and on an outcaste, the wise look with an equal eye.
5.19: Even here, in this life, birth has been conquered by those whose mind rests in evenness;
for Brahman is flawless and the same in all, and so they are established in Brahman.
5.20: He should not rejoice on gaining what is pleasant, nor be troubled on meeting what is unpleasant,
he who is firm of mind and undeluded, who knows Brahman and is established in Brahman.
5.21: One whose mind is not attached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the Self;
he, his mind joined to Brahman in yoga, enjoys happiness that does not decay.
5.22: For the pleasures that are born of contact are only sources of sorrow;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī; the wise man does not delight in them.
5.23: One who is able, even here, before release from the body,
to withstand the surge born of desire and anger is a yogī; he is a happy man.
5.24: He whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light likewise is within alone,
that yogī, having become Brahman, attains brahmanirvāṇa, the final peace in Brahman.
5.25: Brahmanirvāṇa is attained by the seers whose sins are worn away,
whose doubts are cut away, who are self-controlled and delight in the good of all beings.
5.26: For ascetics freed from desire and anger, whose minds are controlled
and who have known the Self, brahmanirvāṇa is present both here and hereafter.
5.27: Keeping outer contacts outside, and the gaze fixed between the brows,
making the outgoing and incoming breaths that move within the nostrils equal,
5.28: the sage whose senses, mind and intellect are restrained, who holds liberation as his highest goal,
and from whom desire, fear and anger have gone, is indeed ever free.
5.29: As the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds,
and the friend of all beings: knowing me so, he attains peace.
5.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fifth chapter, named Saṃnyāsayoga, the yoga of renunciation.
6.1: He who does the work he ought to do, without depending on the fruit of action,
is a renunciant and a yogī too; not the one who has merely given up the ritual fires, nor the one who has merely given up action.
6.2: What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, the discipline of action, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogī without renouncing his intentions.
6.3: For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same sage, once he has ascended to yoga, calm is said to be the means.
6.4: When one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions,
then he who has renounced all intentions is said to have ascended to yoga.
6.5: One should lift oneself up by oneself, and not let oneself sink down;
for the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
6.6: For him by whom the self has been conquered by the self, the self is the friend of the self;
but for one who has not conquered himself, the self itself acts with hostility, like an enemy.
6.7: For one who has conquered himself and is wholly at peace, the supreme Self is steadily present,
in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise in honour and dishonour.
6.8: One whose self is content with knowledge and realised knowledge, who stands unshaken and has conquered his senses,
and for whom a clod, a stone and gold are the same — such a yogī is said to be steadfast in yoga.
6.9: One who has the same mind towards well-wishers, friends and foes, the indifferent and the impartial, the hateful and kinsmen,
and towards the good and the sinful alike, excels.
6.10: The yogī should constantly engage himself in yoga, staying in a secluded place,
alone, with mind and body controlled, free from expectation and owning nothing.
6.11: Having set up for himself, in a clean place, a firm seat,
neither too high nor too low, covered with a cloth, a deerskin and kuśa grass, laid one upon another —
6.12: — there, making the mind one-pointed, with the workings of mind and senses held in check,
seated on that seat, he should practise yoga for the purification of his inner self.
6.13: Holding body, head and neck erect and still, himself steady,
gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in any direction —
6.14: — serene within, rid of fear, firm in the brahmacārī's vow of celibacy,
restraining the mind, with his thought on me, he should sit steadfast in yoga, holding me as the supreme goal.
6.15: Thus always engaging himself in yoga, the yogī of disciplined mind
attains the peace whose highest end is nirvāṇa, final liberation, and which rests in me.
6.16: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all;
nor for one given to too much sleep, nor indeed for one who keeps awake too long, O Arjuna.
6.17: For one who is moderate in food and in moving about, moderate in his efforts in action,
and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
6.18: When the well-restrained mind rests in the Self alone,
and one is free from craving for every desire, then he is said to be steadfast in yoga.
6.19: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the simile handed down
for the yogī of controlled mind who practises the yoga of the Self.
6.20: That state in which the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest,
and in which, seeing the Self through the self, one is content in the Self —
6.21: — that endless happiness which the intellect grasps and which lies beyond the senses,
where he knows it, and where, once established, he never moves from the truth —
6.22: — having gained which he counts no other gain greater than it,
and established in which he is not shaken even by heavy sorrow —
6.23: — that unyoking from union with sorrow, let one know, is what is named yoga.
This yoga is to be practised with resolve and with a mind that does not lose heart.
6.24: Giving up all desires that spring from intention, leaving none behind,
and with the mind alone restraining all the senses on every side,
6.25: one should come to rest little by little, through the intellect held fast by resolve;
having settled the mind in the Self, one should think of nothing at all.
6.26: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off,
from there one should draw it back and bring it under control in the Self alone.
6.27: For supreme happiness comes to this yogī whose mind is wholly at peace,
whose rajas, the guṇa of passion, is stilled, who has become Brahman, the Absolute, and is free from taint.
6.28: Thus ever engaging himself in yoga, the yogī, freed from taint,
easily enjoys the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
6.29: The Self as dwelling in every being, and every being in the Self:
so sees one whose self is joined in yoga, who sees the same everywhere.
6.30: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me —
I am not lost to him, and he is not lost to me.
6.31: One who, established in oneness, worships me as abiding in all beings —
that yogī, however he may live, abides in me.
6.32: One who, taking himself as the measure, sees all alike everywhere, O Arjuna,
be it pleasure or be it pain — that yogī is held to be the highest.
6.33: This yoga which you have taught as evenness of mind, O Madhusūdana —
I do not see its steady continuance, because the mind is restless.
6.34: For the mind is restless, O Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, strong and stubborn;
I think restraining it is extremely hard, like restraining the wind.
6.35: Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is hard to restrain and restless;
but, O son of Kuntī, it is held in check by practice and by dispassion.
6.36: Yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is unrestrained — this is my view;
but one whose self is controlled, and who strives, can attain it by the right means.
6.37: One who has faith but is slack in effort, whose mind has strayed from yoga —
failing to reach perfection in yoga, what end does he come to, O Kṛṣṇa?
6.38: Fallen from both, does he not perish like a cloud torn apart,
without support, O mighty-armed one, bewildered on the path to Brahman?
6.39: This doubt of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, you should cut away entirely;
for no one other than you can be found to cut away this doubt.
6.40: O Pārtha, neither here nor in the world to come is there ruin for him;
for no one who does good, my dear, comes to an evil end.
6.41: Having reached the worlds of those who did good, and dwelt there for countless years,
one who has fallen from yoga is born in the home of the pure and the prosperous.
6.42: Or else he is born into a family of wise yogīs themselves;
such a birth as this is indeed harder to gain in the world.
6.43: There he regains that union with the understanding he had in his former body,
and from there he strives yet more for perfection, O joy of the Kurus.
6.44: By that very former practice he is drawn on towards yoga, even against his will;
even one who only seeks to know yoga goes beyond the Veda, the word-Brahman.
6.45: But the yogī who strives with diligence, cleansed of sins,
perfected through many births, then reaches the supreme goal.
6.46: The yogī is greater than ascetics, and held greater even than men of knowledge;
the yogī is greater, too, than men of ritual action; so, O Arjuna, be a yogī.
6.47: And of all yogīs, the one who, with his inner self absorbed in me, full of faith,
worships me — he, I hold, is the most steadfast in yoga.
6.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the sixth chapter, named Ātmasaṃyamayoga, the yoga of self-control.
7.1: With your mind attached to me, O Pārtha, practising yoga, the discipline of the mind, with me as your refuge,
hear how you will know me in full, without doubt.
7.2: I shall declare to you in full this knowledge together with realised knowledge,
knowing which nothing further remains here to be known.
7.3: Out of thousands of men, perhaps one strives for perfection;
and even among the perfected who strive, perhaps one knows me in truth.
7.4: Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind and intellect,
and ego: thus is this prakṛti of mine, my nature, divided eightfold.
7.5: This is the lower; but know my other, higher nature, distinct from this,
which is the jīva, the living self, O mighty-armed one, by which this world is upheld.
7.6: Understand that all beings have these two natures as their source.
I am the origin of the whole world, and likewise its dissolution.
7.7: There is nothing whatever higher than me, O Dhanañjaya.
All this is strung on me like clusters of gems on a thread.
7.8: In water I am the taste, O son of Kuntī; in the moon and the sun I am the light;
the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, the manliness in men.
7.9: I am the pure fragrance in the earth, and I am the brilliance in fire;
I am the life in all beings, and the austerity in ascetics.
7.10: Know me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings.
Of the intelligent I am the intelligence; of the brilliant, the brilliance.
7.11: And of the strong I am the strength that is free from desire and attachment;
in beings I am the desire that is not opposed to dharma, right conduct, O best of the Bharatas.
7.12: And whatever states of being are of sattva, and those that are of rajas and of tamas,
know them to have come from me alone; yet I am not in them, they are in me.
7.13: By these three states made of the guṇas, the three qualities of nature, this whole world
is deluded and does not know me, the imperishable one beyond them.
7.14: For this divine māyā of mine, my power of illusion, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross;
those who take refuge in me alone cross over this māyā.
7.15: Evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men do not take refuge in me,
they whose knowledge māyā has taken away, who have resorted to the demonic nature.
7.16: Four kinds of people who do good deeds worship me, O Arjuna:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, O best of the Bharatas.
7.17: Of them the wise one, ever steadfast, devoted to the One alone, excels;
for to the wise I am dear beyond measure, and he is dear to me.
7.18: All these are noble, but the wise one is my very Self; such is my view.
For he, steadfast in mind, is established in me alone, the unsurpassed goal.
7.19: At the end of many births the man of knowledge takes refuge in me,
knowing that Vāsudeva is all; such a great soul is very rare.
7.20: Those whose knowledge has been carried away by this desire or that take refuge in other deities,
adopting this or that observance, governed by their own nature.
7.21: Whatever divine form any devotee wishes to worship with faith,
that very faith of each I make unwavering.
7.22: Endowed with that faith, he seeks to worship that form,
and from it obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by me alone.
7.23: But the fruit that comes to those of small understanding is finite.
Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
7.24: The unintelligent believe that I, the unmanifest, have come into manifestation,
unaware of my supreme nature, imperishable and unsurpassed.
7.25: I am not manifest to all, being veiled by yogamāyā;
this deluded world does not know me, the unborn and imperishable.
7.26: I know the beings of the past and of the present, O Arjuna,
and those yet to come; but no one knows me.
7.27: Through the delusion of the pairs of opposites, born of desire and aversion, O Bhārata,
all beings fall into utter bewilderment at birth, O scorcher of foes.
7.28: But those whose sin has ended, people of virtuous deeds,
freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship me, firm in their vows.
7.29: Those who, taking refuge in me, strive for release from old age and death,
know that Brahman; they know adhyātma, the inner self, in full, and karma, action, in its entirety.
7.30: Those who know me together with the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva, and with the adhiyajña,
know me, their minds steadfast, even at the time of departure.
7.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the seventh chapter, named Jñānavijñānayoga, the yoga of knowledge and realised knowledge.
8.1: What is that Brahman? What is adhyātma? What is karma, O Supreme Person?
And what is said to be adhibhūta? What is called adhidaiva?
8.2: Who is the adhiyajña here in this body, and how is he in it, O Madhusūdana?
And at the time of departure, how are you to be known by those who are self-controlled?
8.3: The supreme Imperishable is Brahman; its own being, as the self in each body, is called adhyātma.
The visarga, the offering to the gods, which brings beings into existence, is called karma.
8.4: Adhibhūta is the perishable existence, and the Puruṣa is adhidaivata;
the adhiyajña here in this body is I myself, O best of the embodied.
8.5: And whoever at the time of the end, remembering me alone, leaves the body
and departs, attains my being; of this there is no doubt.
8.6: Or whatever state of being one remembers as one gives up the body at the end,
to that alone one goes, O son of Kuntī, having always been absorbed in that state.
8.7: Therefore at all times remember me, and fight.
With your mind and intellect offered to me, you will come to me alone, without doubt.
8.8: With a mind joined in the yoga of practice and turning to nothing else,
meditating constantly, O Pārtha, one goes to the supreme, divine Person.
8.9: Whoever remembers the all-knowing Seer, the Ancient, the Ruler,
the ordainer of all, whose form is beyond thought,
shining like the sun, beyond darkness —
8.10: At the hour of death, with an unmoving mind,
joined to devotion and to the power of yoga, the discipline of the mind,
having set the life-breath fully between the eyebrows,
he reaches that supreme, divine Person.
8.11: That which the knowers of the Veda call the Imperishable,
which ascetics free from passion enter,
desiring which men keep brahmacarya, the life of celibate study,
that goal I shall declare to you in brief.
8.12: Restraining all the gates of the senses, confining the mind within the heart,
placing his own life-breath in the head, set firm in the concentration of yoga —
8.13: uttering Om, the one syllable that is Brahman, the Absolute, and remembering me,
whoever departs, leaving the body, reaches the supreme goal.
8.14: He who, with his mind on nothing else, remembers me constantly, all his life —
for that yogī, ever steadfast, I am easily reached, O Pārtha.
8.15: Having reached me, they do not come again to birth, the home of sorrow, which does not last;
these great-souled ones have attained the highest perfection.
8.16: From all the worlds, up to the world of Brahmā, there is return, O Arjuna;
but for one who reaches me, O son of Kuntī, there is no birth again.
8.17: Those who know that a day of Brahmā lasts a thousand yugas, ages of the world,
and that his night ends after a thousand yugas, are the people who know day and night.
8.18: All manifest things spring from the unmanifest at the coming of Brahmā's day;
at the coming of night they dissolve into that very thing which is called the unmanifest.
8.19: This same multitude of beings, coming into being again and again,
dissolves helplessly at the coming of night, O Pārtha, and springs forth at the coming of day.
8.20: But higher than that unmanifest there is another being, unmanifest and eternal,
which does not perish when all beings perish.
8.21: This unmanifest is called the Imperishable; it is what they call the supreme goal.
Those who reach it do not return; that is my supreme abode.
8.22: That supreme Person, O Pārtha, is to be won by undivided devotion,
he within whom beings abide, by whom all this is pervaded.
8.23: Now the time at which yogīs go to no return, and also to return,
when they depart — that time I shall tell you, O best of the Bharatas.
8.24: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northward course:
departing on this path, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
8.25: Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southward course:
on this path the yogī reaches the light of the moon, and comes back.
8.26: These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are indeed held to be eternal;
taking the one, a person goes to no return; taking the other, he comes back again.
8.27: Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogī whatever is deluded.
Therefore at all times be steadfast in yoga, O Arjuna.
8.28: For the Vedas, for sacrifices, for austerities
and for gifts, whatever fruit of merit is declared —
having known this, the yogī goes beyond all that,
and reaches the supreme, primal abode.
8.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eighth chapter, named Akṣarabrahmayoga, the yoga of the imperishable Brahman.
9.1: But to you, who do not find fault, I shall declare this most secret knowledge, together with realised knowledge,
knowing which you will be freed from evil.
9.2: This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, the supreme purifier;
it is known by direct experience, it is righteous, it is very easy to practise, and it does not perish.
9.3: Men who have no faith in this dharma, this sacred path, O scorcher of foes,
do not reach me, and return to the path of worldly existence, which is full of death.
9.4: All this world is pervaded by me, whose form is unmanifest;
all beings abide in me, but I do not abide in them.
9.5: And yet beings do not abide in me: behold my lordly power of yoga.
My Self sustains beings and brings them into being, yet does not abide in beings.
9.6: As the mighty wind, moving everywhere, rests always in space,
so understand that all beings rest in me.
9.7: All beings, O son of Kuntī, pass into my prakṛti, my own nature, at the end of a kalpa, a cycle of creation;
at the beginning of a kalpa I send them forth again.
9.8: Keeping my own prakṛti under my control, again and again I send forth
this whole multitude of beings, helpless under the sway of prakṛti.
9.9: And those acts do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya;
I sit like one indifferent, unattached to those acts.
9.10: With me as overseer, prakṛti brings forth all that moves and does not move;
for this reason, O son of Kuntī, the world goes round.
9.11: The deluded disregard me when I have taken a human body,
not knowing my supreme nature as the great Lord of beings.
9.12: Vain in their hopes, vain in their acts, vain in their knowledge, senseless,
they have taken to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras, the demons.
9.13: But the great-souled, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in the divine nature,
worship me with minds turned to nothing else, knowing me as the imperishable origin of beings.
9.14: Always singing my praise and striving, firm in their vows,
and bowing to me in devotion, ever steadfast, they worship me.
9.15: Others too, offering the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me —
in oneness, in distinctness and in many forms, me whose face is everywhere.
9.16: I am the Vedic rite, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the herb;
I am the mantra, I myself am the clarified butter, I am the fire, I am the act of offering.
9.17: I am the father of this world, its mother, its ordainer, its grandsire;
I am what is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om, and the Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda and the Yajurveda as well.
9.18: I am the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend;
the origin and the dissolution, the resting place, the treasure-house, the seed that does not perish.
9.19: I give heat; I hold back the rain and I send it forth;
I am immortality and also death, being and non-being, O Arjuna.
9.20: Those who know the three Vedas, who drink the soma and are cleansed of sin,
having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven;
reaching the holy world of Indra, lord of the gods,
they enjoy in heaven the divine pleasures of the gods.
9.21: Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is spent.
Thus those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas, the rites they enjoin,
desiring the objects of desire, gain going and coming.
9.22: Those people who, with no other thought, meditate on me and worship me in every way —
for them, ever steadfast, I carry the gaining of what they lack and the keeping of what they have.
9.23: Even those devotees who worship other gods, endowed with faith,
they too worship me alone, O son of Kuntī, though not by the rule laid down.
9.24: For I am the enjoyer and indeed the lord of all sacrifices;
but they do not know me in truth, and therefore they fall.
9.25: Those whose vows are to the gods go to the gods; those whose vows are to the ancestors go to the ancestors;
worshippers of spirits go to the spirits; and those who worship me come to me.
9.26: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water,
I partake of that offering made with devotion by one pure in mind.
9.27: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer into the fire, whatever you give,
whatever austerity you practise, O son of Kuntī, make it an offering to me.
9.28: Thus you will be freed from the bonds of action, which bear good and evil fruits;
with your mind joined in the yoga of renunciation, set free, you will come to me.
9.29: I am the same towards all beings; none is hateful to me, none dear.
But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I too am in them.
9.30: Even if a man of very evil conduct worships me, devoted to no other,
he is to be regarded as good, for he has resolved rightly.
9.31: Quickly he becomes righteous in soul and reaches lasting peace.
O son of Kuntī, declare it for certain: my devotee never perishes.
9.32: For, O Pārtha, those who take refuge in me, even those who may be of sinful birth,
and women, vaiśyas and śūdras too, reach the supreme goal.
9.33: How much more, then, holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal sages!
Having come to this transient, joyless world, worship me.
9.34: Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, bow down to me.
Having thus steadied yourself, with me as your supreme goal, you will come to me alone.
9.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the ninth chapter, named Rājavidyārājaguhyayoga, the yoga of the sovereign knowledge and the sovereign secret.
10.1: Once more, O mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word,
which I shall speak to you, who take delight in it, out of a wish for your welfare.
10.2: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great sages know my origin,
for I am in every way the source of the gods and of the great sages.
10.3: He who knows me as unborn and without beginning, the great Lord of the worlds,
is undeluded among mortals and is freed from all sins.
10.4: Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forbearance, truth, restraint of the senses, calm of mind,
pleasure, pain, coming into being, ceasing to be, fear and also fearlessness,
10.5: non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, giving, fame and ill fame —
these states of beings, of many kinds, arise from me alone.
10.6: The seven great sages of old and likewise the four Manus,
sharing my nature, were born from my mind; theirs are these creatures in the world.
10.7: He who knows in truth this glory of mine and my yoga, my sovereign power,
is joined in unwavering yoga; of this there is no doubt.
10.8: I am the origin of all; from me everything goes forth.
Knowing this, the wise worship me, filled with devotion.
10.9: Their minds on me, their lives given to me, making me known to one another
and ever speaking of me, they are content and they rejoice.
10.10: To them, ever steadfast, who worship me with love,
I give that yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
10.11: Out of compassion for them alone, the darkness born of ignorance
I destroy, dwelling within their inner being, with the shining lamp of knowledge.
10.12: You are the supreme Brahman, the Absolute, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier;
the eternal divine Person, the first of the gods, unborn, all-pervading —
10.13: so all the sages call you, and likewise the divine sage Nārada,
Asita, Devala and Vyāsa; and you yourself tell me so.
10.14: All this that you tell me, O Keśava, I hold to be true;
for neither the gods nor the demons know your manifestation, O Lord.
10.15: You yourself alone know yourself through yourself, O Supreme Person,
O source of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Lord of the world.
10.16: You should describe in full your own glories, for they are divine —
the glories by which you abide, pervading these worlds.
10.17: How may I know you, O Yogī, ever meditating on you?
And in what various things are you to be thought of by me, O Lord?
10.18: In detail, O Janārdana, of your own yoga and glory
tell me once more; for as I hear this nectar, I am not sated.
10.19: Very well, I shall tell you of my divine glories,
the chief ones, O best of the Kurus; for there is no end to my extent.
10.20: I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, that dwells in the heart of every being;
I am also the beginning, the middle and the end of beings.
10.21: Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among lights, the radiant sun;
I am Marīci among the Maruts; among the stars I am the moon.
10.22: Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods I am Indra;
among the senses I am the mind; in beings I am consciousness.
10.23: Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara; among the yakṣas and demons, Kubera, the lord of wealth;
among the Vasus I am Agni; among peaked mountains I am Meru.
10.24: And among household priests, O Pārtha, know me as their chief, Bṛhaspati;
among the leaders of armies I am Skanda; among waters I am the ocean.
10.25: Among the great sages I am Bhṛgu; among words I am the one syllable, Om;
among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of japa, the repetition of a sacred word; among things that do not move, the Himālaya.
10.26: Among all trees I am the Aśvattha, the sacred fig, and among the divine sages Nārada;
among the gandharvas I am Citraratha, and among the siddhas, the perfected ones, the sage Kapila.
10.27: Among horses know me as Uccaiḥśravas, born of the churning for the nectar;
among lordly elephants know me as Airāvata, and among men as the king.
10.28: Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows I am Kāmadhuk, the wish-yielding cow;
I am Kandarpa, the god of love who begets offspring; among serpents I am Vāsuki.
10.29: Among the nāgas I am Ananta; among the dwellers of the waters I am Varuṇa;
among the ancestors I am Aryaman, and among those who hold in check I am Yama.
10.30: Among the daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon I am time;
among beasts I am the lion, and among birds Vainateya, Garuḍa the son of Vinatā.
10.31: Among purifiers I am the wind; among those who bear weapons I am Rāma;
among fishes I am the makara, and among rivers I am Jāhnavī, the Gaṅgā.
10.32: Of creations I am the beginning and the end, O Arjuna, and the middle as well.
Among sciences I am the science of the Self; among those who debate I am the reasoning that seeks the truth.
10.33: Among letters I am the letter a, and among compounds the dvandva, the copulative compound.
I alone am imperishable time; I am the ordainer, facing in every direction.
10.34: I am death that seizes all, and the rise of those whose rise is yet to come.
Among the feminine I am fame, fortune and speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and forbearance.
10.35: Among the Sāman chants, too, I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among metres I am the Gāyatrī;
among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons, the spring rich in flowers.
10.36: Of those who cheat I am gambling; of the splendid I am the splendour.
I am victory, I am resolve; of the good I am the goodness.
10.37: Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya;
among sages too I am Vyāsa; among seers, the seer Uśanā, Śukra.
10.38: Of those who subdue I am the rod of punishment; of those who seek victory I am statecraft;
among secret things I am silence, and of the knowing I am knowledge.
10.39: And whatever is the seed of all beings, that I am, O Arjuna.
There is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist without me.
10.40: There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of foes.
This account of their extent I have given only in brief, by way of example.
10.41: Whatever being there is that is glorious, prosperous or mighty,
know every such one to have sprung from a fraction of my splendour.
10.42: Or rather, what use is it to you, O Arjuna, to know all this at length?
I stand, holding up this whole world with a single portion of myself.
10.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the tenth chapter, named Vibhūtiyoga, the yoga of the divine manifestations.
11.1: Out of grace towards me you have spoken the supreme secret word known as adhyātma, the teaching about the Self;
by that word this delusion of mine is gone.
11.2: For I have heard in detail of the origin and the dissolution of beings,
heard them from you, O lotus-eyed one, and of your imperishable greatness too.
11.3: It is so, O Supreme Lord, just as you have declared yourself to be.
Yet I wish to see your sovereign form, O Supreme Person.
11.4: If you think, O Lord, that it can be seen by me,
then, O Lord of yoga, show me yourself, the imperishable.
11.5: Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and by the thousands,
of many kinds, divine, of many colours and shapes.
11.6: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts too;
behold many wonders never seen before, O Bhārata.
11.7: Behold today the whole universe, with all that moves and does not move, gathered here in one place
in my body, O Guḍākeśa, and whatever else you wish to see.
11.8: But you cannot see me with this very eye of your own.
I give you a divine eye; behold my sovereign yoga, my power as the Lord.
11.9: Then, O king, having spoken thus, Hari, the great Lord of yoga,
showed Pārtha his supreme, sovereign form.
11.10: That form had many mouths and eyes and many wondrous sights,
many divine ornaments, and many divine weapons held aloft.
11.11: The God he showed wore divine garlands and garments and was anointed with divine perfumes;
he was full of every wonder, infinite, facing in every direction.
11.12: If the light of a thousand suns were to rise in the sky all at once,
that might perhaps be like the splendour of that great-souled one.
11.13: There the whole universe, divided in many ways, stood gathered in one place;
the son of Pāṇḍu saw it then in the body of the God of gods.
11.14: Then Dhanañjaya was filled with wonder, his hair standing on end;
bowing his head to the God, with joined palms, he spoke.
11.15: In your body, O God, I see the gods,
all of them, and the hosts of every kind of being;
Brahmā the lord, seated on the lotus,
and all the sages and the divine serpents.
11.16: With many arms, bellies, mouths and eyes,
I see you, endless in form on every side;
no end, no middle, nor yet your beginning
do I see, O Lord of the universe, O you whose form is the universe.
11.17: Wearing a crown, bearing a mace and a discus,
a mass of radiance shining on every side,
I see you, hard to look upon from all around,
with the brilliance of blazing fire and the sun, immeasurable.
11.18: You are the Imperishable, the supreme, the one to be known;
you are the supreme resting-place of this universe;
you are undying, the guardian of the eternal dharma, the order of right;
you, I hold, are the eternal Person.
11.19: Without beginning, middle or end, of infinite power,
with countless arms, the moon and the sun your eyes,
I see you, your mouth a blazing fire,
scorching this universe with your own radiance.
11.20: For this space between heaven and earth is filled
by you alone, and so is every direction.
At the sight of this wondrous and terrible form of yours,
the three worlds are deeply shaken, O great-souled one.
11.21: These hosts of gods are entering into you;
some, in fear, extol you with joined palms.
Saying svasti, may it be well, the hosts of great sages and siddhas
praise you with hymns rich and full.
11.22: The Rudras and the Ādityas, the Vasus and the Sādhyas,
the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts and the Ūṣmapas, a class of ancestors,
and the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras and siddhas
all gaze at you in amazement.
11.23: Your mighty form has many mouths and eyes;
O mighty-armed one, it has many arms, thighs and feet,
many bellies, and is terrible with many tusks;
seeing it, the worlds are terrified, and so am I.
11.24: You touch the sky, blazing, of many colours;
your mouths gape wide, your huge eyes blaze.
Seeing you so, I am shaken in my inmost self,
and I find neither steadiness nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
11.25: And your mouths are terrible with tusks
and like the fire of the final dissolution; merely seeing them,
I no longer know the directions, and I find no comfort.
Be gracious, O Lord of gods, abode of the world.
11.26: all of them, together with the hosts of kings,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that charioteer's son Karṇa as well,
together with the chief warriors of our own side too,
11.27: are rushing into you, into your mouths,
Some are seen caught in the gaps between the teeth,
11.28: As the many torrents of rivers
rush on, facing the ocean alone,
so these heroes of the world of men
enter your mouths, flaming all around.
11.29: As moths enter a blazing fire
with gathering speed, to their destruction,
so too the worlds enter, to their destruction,
your mouths as well, with gathering speed.
11.30: Licking again and again, you devour on every side
all the worlds with your flaming mouths.
Filling the whole universe with brilliance,
your fierce rays scorch it, O Viṣṇu.
11.31: Tell me who you are, of so fierce a form.
Salutation to you, O best of gods; be gracious.
I wish to know you fully, the Primal One,
for I do not understand what you are doing.
11.32: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of the worlds,
engaged here in annihilating the worlds.
Even without you, none of them will survive,
the warriors who stand arrayed in the opposing armies.
11.33: conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These have already been slain by me alone;
be merely the instrument, O ambidextrous archer.
11.34: Karṇa, and the other heroic warriors too,
already slain by me, you must slay; do not be distressed.
Fight: you will conquer your rivals in battle.
11.35: the diademed Arjuna, palms joined and trembling,
saluted him and spoke again to Kṛṣṇa,
in a faltering voice, utterly afraid, bowing low.
11.36: It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that at the singing of your glory
the world rejoices and is drawn to you in love;
the demons flee in fear in all directions,
and all the hosts of siddhas, the perfected ones, bow to you.
11.37: And why should they not bow to you, O great-souled one,
who are greater than all, the first creator even of Brahmā?
O Infinite One, Lord of gods, abode of the world,
you are the Imperishable: being and non-being, and that which is beyond them.
11.38: You are the first God, the ancient Person;
you are the supreme resting-place of this universe.
You are the knower and what is to be known, and the supreme abode;
the universe is pervaded by you, O you of infinite forms.
11.39: You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the moon,
Salutations, salutations to you a thousand times;
and again, and yet again, salutations, salutations to you.
11.40: Salutation to you in front and behind;
salutation to you on every side, O All.
You are infinite in strength and boundless in valour;
you pervade everything wholly; therefore you are all.
11.41: Whatever I have said presumptuously, thinking you a friend,
not knowing this greatness of yours,
out of carelessness, or even out of affection,
11.42: and whatever disrespect you were shown in jest,
at play, at rest, when seated or at meals,
alone, O Acyuta, or in the presence of others:
for that I ask forgiveness of you, the Immeasurable.
11.43: You are the father of this world, of all that moves and does not move;
you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher.
There is none equal to you; how then could another be greater?
Not even in the three worlds, O you of matchless power.
11.44: Therefore, bowing down and laying my body low,
I seek the grace of you, the Lord, worthy of praise.
As a father bears with his son, a friend with his friend,
and a lover with his beloved, so should you bear with me, O God.
11.45: I rejoice at having seen what was never seen before,
and yet my mind is shaken with fear.
Show me that same form of yours, O God;
be gracious, O Lord of gods, abode of the world.
11.46: Crowned, bearing the mace, with the discus in hand,
I wish to see you, just as before.
Take on that same four-armed form,
O thousand-armed one, O you whose form is the universe.
11.47: Pleased with you, O Arjuna, I have shown you
this supreme form by my own power of yoga:
a form of mine that no one but you has seen before.
11.48: Not by the study of the Vedas and of sacrifices, not by gifts,
nor by rites, nor by severe austerities
can I be seen in such a form in the world of men
by anyone other than you, O great hero of the Kurus.
11.49: Let there be no distress for you, and no bewilderment,
at seeing this terrible form of mine, such as it is.
Free from fear and glad at heart, once more
behold that same form of mine: here it is.
11.50: Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva
showed his own form once more,
and the great-souled one consoled the frightened Arjuna,
becoming once again gentle in form.
11.51: Seeing this gentle human form of yours, O Janārdana,
I have now come to my senses and returned to my natural state.
11.52: This form of mine that you have seen is very hard to behold;
even the gods ever long for a sight of this form.
11.53: Not by the Vedas, not by austerity, not by gifts, nor by sacrifice
can I be seen in the form in which you have seen me.
11.54: But by undivided devotion, O Arjuna, I can be known in this form,
and seen as I truly am, and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
11.55: He who does his work for me, for whom I am the highest, who is devoted to me, free from attachment
and without enmity towards any being, comes to me, O Pāṇḍava.
11.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eleventh chapter, named Viśvarūpadarśanayoga, the yoga of the vision of the universal form.
12.1: Those devotees who, ever steadfast in this way, worship you,
and those who worship the Imperishable, the Unmanifest: which of them know yoga best?
12.2: Those who fix their mind on me and worship me, ever steadfast,
endowed with supreme faith: they, in my view, are the most perfect in yoga.
12.3: But those who worship the Imperishable, the Indefinable, the Unmanifest,
the All-pervading, the Unthinkable, the Changeless, the Unmoving, the Eternal,
12.4: who have fully restrained all the senses and are even-minded everywhere,
rejoicing in the good of all beings: it is me that they reach.
12.5: The toil is far greater for those whose minds are set on the Unmanifest;
for the unmanifest goal is reached with pain by embodied beings.
12.6: But those who surrender all their actions to me, intent on me,
and worship me, meditating on me with yoga that is undivided,
12.7: for them, whose minds are fixed on me, I become before long the deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence bound to death, O Pārtha.
12.8: Fix your mind on me alone; settle your intellect in me.
Thereafter you will dwell in me alone; of this there is no doubt.
12.9: If, however, you cannot fix your mind steadily on me,
then seek to reach me through the yoga of practice, O Dhanañjaya.
12.10: If even practice is beyond your power, give yourself wholly to work for me;
you will reach perfection even by doing actions for my sake.
12.11: If you are unable to do even this, then, taking refuge in my yoga,
and self-controlled, give up the fruits of all actions.
12.12: Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation excels knowledge;
giving up the fruits of action excels meditation; from giving up, peace follows at once.
12.13: He who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate,
