free from possessiveness and from ego, alike in sorrow and joy, forgiving,
12.14: ever content, a yogī, self-controlled, firm in resolve,
with mind and intellect offered to me — he who is my devotee is dear to me.
12.15: He who gives the world no cause for agitation, and whom the world does not agitate,
who is free from elation, intolerance, fear and agitation — he too is dear to me.
12.16: He who has no expectations, who is pure, capable, impartial, untroubled,
who has given up all undertakings — he who is my devotee is dear to me.
12.17: He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor craves,
who has given up both good and evil, and is full of devotion — that one is dear to me.
12.18: The same towards enemy and friend, and so too in honour and disgrace,
the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, free from attachment,
12.19: the same in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes,
without a fixed home, steady-minded, full of devotion — that man is dear to me.
12.20: But those who follow this righteous nectar just as it has been taught,
full of faith, holding me as supreme — those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
12.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the twelfth chapter, named Bhaktiyoga, the yoga of devotion.
13.1: Prakṛti, primal nature, and puruṣa, the conscious self; the field and the knower of the field;
knowledge and what is to be known: this I wish to know, O Keśava.
13.2: This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field;
those versed in this call the one who knows it the knower of the field.
13.3: Know me also, O Bhārata, as the knower of the field in all fields.
The knowledge of the field and of its knower: that, in my view, is knowledge.
13.4: What that field is, what it is like, what its modifications are, and what arises from what;
and who he, the knower, is and what his powers are: hear that from me in brief.
13.5: It has been sung by the seers in many ways, distinctly in various Vedic hymns,
and also in the passages that point to Brahman, well reasoned and conclusive.
13.6: The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect and the unmanifest too;
the ten senses and the one mind, and the five objects of the senses;
13.7: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the bodily aggregate, awareness and fortitude:
this, in brief, is declared to be the field together with its modifications.
13.8: Absence of pride, absence of pretence, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness,
service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-restraint;
13.9: dispassion towards the objects of the senses, and absence of egoism;
seeing again and again the evil in birth, death, old age, disease and pain;
13.10: non-attachment, no clinging to son, wife, home and the like,
and constant evenness of mind whether the desired or the undesired befalls;
13.11: unswerving devotion to me through undivided yoga;
resorting to solitary places, and no delight in crowds of people;
13.12: constancy in knowledge of the Self, and keeping in sight the goal of knowing the truth:
this is declared to be knowledge; what is contrary to it is ignorance.
13.13: I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality:
the beginningless supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
13.14: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere,
with ears everywhere, it abides in the world, enveloping all.
13.15: It shines through the functions of all the senses, yet is devoid of all senses;
unattached, yet sustaining all; without the guṇas, the qualities of nature, yet the experiencer of the guṇas.
13.16: It is outside and inside beings, unmoving and also moving;
because of its subtlety it cannot be known; it is far away and also near.
13.17: Undivided, it abides in beings as if divided;
and that knowable is the sustainer of beings, their devourer and their creator.
13.18: It is the light even of lights, and is spoken of as beyond darkness;
it is knowledge, the knowable and what is reached by knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
13.19: Thus the field, and knowledge and the knowable too, have been told in brief.
When my devotee has understood this, he becomes fit for my being.
13.20: Know that prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless;
and know that the modifications and the guṇas are born of prakṛti.
13.21: Prakṛti is said to be the cause in the producing of effect and cause;
puruṣa is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasures and pains.
13.22: For puruṣa, abiding in prakṛti, experiences the guṇas born of prakṛti;
its attachment to the guṇas is what causes it to be born in good and evil wombs.
13.23: The witness and the permitter, the sustainer, the experiencer, the great Lord,
and also the supreme Self: so the supreme puruṣa in this body is called.
13.24: He who thus knows puruṣa, and prakṛti together with the guṇas,
in whatever way he may be living, is not born again.
13.25: Some, through meditation, see the Self in the self by the self;
others through the yoga of Sāṅkhya, and still others through the yoga of action.
13.26: But others, not knowing the Self in this way, hear of it from others and worship;
they too, devoted to what they have heard, surely cross beyond death.
13.27: Whatever being comes into existence, unmoving or moving,
know that it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field, O best of the Bharatas.
13.28: He who sees the supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings,
the imperishable among the perishing, he truly sees.
13.29: For, seeing with an even eye the Lord who abides equally everywhere,
he does not harm the Self by the self; therefore he goes to the supreme goal.
13.30: He who sees that all actions are performed in every way by prakṛti alone,
and likewise sees the Self as not the doer, he truly sees.
13.31: When one sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the One,
and their spreading out from that One alone, then one becomes Brahman, the Absolute.
13.32: Being without beginning and free from the guṇas, this imperishable supreme Self,
though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, neither acts nor is tainted.
13.33: As all-pervading space, being subtle, is not tainted,
so the Self, present everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
13.34: As the one sun lights up this whole world,
so, O Bhārata, the owner of the field lights up the whole field.
13.35: Those who thus know, with the eye of knowledge, how the field differs from the knower of the field,
and know the release from prakṛti, the source of beings, go to the Supreme.
13.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the thirteenth chapter, named Kṣetrakṣetrajñavibhāgayoga, the yoga of the distinction between the field and its knower.
14.1: Once more I shall declare the supreme knowledge, the highest of all knowledge,
knowing which all the sages have passed from here to the supreme perfection.
14.2: Taking refuge in this knowledge, those who have attained my own nature
are not born even at the creation, nor are they troubled at the dissolution.
14.3: My womb is the great Brahman (prakṛti, primal nature); in it I place the seed.
From that, O Bhārata, all beings come to birth.
14.4: Whatever bodies come into being in all wombs, O son of Kuntī,
the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the father who gives the seed.
14.5: Sattva, rajas and tamas — these guṇas, the qualities born of prakṛti,
bind fast in the body, O mighty-armed one, the imperishable embodied one.
14.6: Of these, sattva, being stainless, is illuminating and free from ill;
it binds, O sinless one, by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge.
14.7: Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, the source of craving and attachment;
it binds the embodied one, O son of Kuntī, by attachment to action.
14.8: But know tamas to be born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings;
it binds, O Bhārata, by heedlessness, sloth and sleep.
14.9: Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, O Bhārata;
but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to heedlessness.
14.10: Sattva prevails, O Bhārata, overpowering rajas and tamas;
rajas prevails, overpowering sattva and tamas; and likewise tamas, overpowering sattva and rajas.
14.11: When in all the gates of this body light arises, the light of knowledge,
then one should know that sattva has increased.
14.12: Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness and longing:
these arise when rajas has increased, O best of the Bharatas.
14.13: Darkness, inactivity, heedlessness and delusion too:
these arise when tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus.
14.14: When sattva has increased and the embodied one dies at that time,
he then attains the stainless worlds of the knowers of the highest.
14.15: When death comes to him while rajas prevails, he is born among those who cling to action;
and likewise, when he dies while tamas prevails, he is born in the wombs of the deluded.
14.16: The fruit of good action, they say, is sāttvika and stainless;
but the fruit of rajas is sorrow, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
14.17: From sattva arises knowledge, and from rajas greed;
from tamas come heedlessness and delusion, and ignorance as well.
14.18: Those established in sattva go upward; those of rajas remain in the middle;
those of tamas, abiding in the workings of the lowest guṇa, go downward.
14.19: When the seer beholds no doer other than the guṇas
and knows that which is beyond the guṇas, he attains my being.
14.20: Having gone beyond these three guṇas, from which the body arises, the embodied one,
freed from birth, death, old age and sorrow, attains immortality.
14.21: By what marks is one known who has gone beyond these three guṇas, O Lord?
How does he conduct himself, and how does he pass beyond these three guṇas?
14.22: Light, activity and delusion, O Pāṇḍava:
he who does not hate them when they arise, nor longs for them when they cease;
14.23: who, seated like one indifferent, is not shaken by the guṇas;
who, knowing thus that the guṇas are at work, stays firm and does not stir;
14.24: who is alike in sorrow and joy, abides in the Self, and holds a clod, a stone and gold as equal;
who is the same towards the pleasant and the unpleasant, wise, the same in blame and in praise of himself;
14.25: who is the same in honour and dishonour, the same to the side of friend and of foe,
and has given up every undertaking — he is said to have gone beyond the guṇas.
14.26: And he who serves me with the yoga of devotion that never wavers
goes fully beyond these guṇas and becomes fit to become Brahman.
14.27: For I am the foundation of Brahman, the immortal and imperishable,
of dharma, the eternal law, and of unfailing bliss.
14.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fourteenth chapter, named Guṇatrayavibhāgayoga, the yoga of the division of the three guṇas.
15.1: They speak of an imperishable aśvattha, the sacred fig tree, with its roots above and its branches below;
its leaves are the Vedic hymns; he who knows it knows the Veda.
15.2: Its branches spread below and above,
nourished by the guṇas, the three qualities of nature, with sense-objects as their shoots;
and below, its roots stretch on and on,
binding to action in the world of humans.
15.3: Its form is not perceived here as it has been described,
nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its continuance.
Having cut down this aśvattha, its roots grown firm and deep,
with the strong weapon of non-attachment —
15.4: one must then seek that state
having gone to which they do not return again,
with the thought: I take refuge in that primal Person alone,
from whom this ancient stream of activity has flowed forth.
15.5: Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment,
ever intent on the Self, with desires wholly turned away,
freed from the dualities called pleasure and pain,
the undeluded reach that imperishable state.
15.6: Neither the sun illumines it, nor the moon, nor fire;
having gone there, they do not return: that is my supreme abode.
15.7: An eternal portion of myself alone, having become the individual soul in the world of living beings,
draws to itself the five senses and the mind, the sixth, which abide in prakṛti, primal nature.
15.8: When the lord of the body acquires a body, and when he departs from it,
he takes these with him and goes, as the wind takes scents from their source.
15.9: The ear, the eye, the skin, the tongue and the nose —
over these and over the mind he presides, and so enjoys the objects of the senses.
15.10: Whether he departs, or stays, or enjoys, joined with the guṇas,
the deluded do not see him; those who have the eye of knowledge see him.
15.11: Yogīs who strive see him dwelling in themselves;
but those whose minds are not disciplined, lacking discernment, do not see him, even though they strive.
15.12: The radiance that is in the sun and lights up the whole world,
and that which is in the moon and in fire — know that radiance to be mine.
15.13: And entering the earth, I uphold beings by my power;
and becoming Soma, the moon, whose essence is sap, I nourish all the plants.
15.14: Becoming Vaiśvānara, the fire of digestion, I dwell in the bodies of living beings,
and joined with the vital breaths prāṇa and apāna, I digest the four kinds of food.
15.15: And I am seated in the heart of all;
from me arise memory and knowledge, and their loss.
I alone am what is to be known through all the Vedas;
I am the maker of Vedānta, and I am indeed the knower of the Vedas.
15.16: These two persons are in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the unchanging one is called the imperishable.
15.17: But the highest Person is another, called the Supreme Self,
who, the imperishable Lord, enters the three worlds and upholds them.
15.18: Since I am beyond the perishable and higher even than the imperishable,
I am therefore known in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
15.19: He who, undeluded, thus knows me as the Supreme Person,
knows all, and worships me with his whole being, O Bhārata.
15.20: Thus I have spoken this most secret teaching, O sinless one.
Understanding it, one becomes wise and has done all there is to do, O Bhārata.
15.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the fifteenth chapter, named Puruṣottamayoga, the yoga of the Supreme Person.
16.1: Fearlessness, complete purity of mind, steadfastness in knowledge and in yoga, the discipline of the mind,
charity, self-restraint and sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, uprightness,
16.2: non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquillity, absence of slander,
compassion towards beings, freedom from craving, gentleness, modesty, absence of fickleness,
16.3: vigour, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice, freedom from excessive pride —
these belong to one born to the divine endowment, O Bhārata.
16.4: Hypocrisy, arrogance and conceit, anger, and harshness too,
and ignorance — these belong to one born to the demonic endowment, O Pārtha.
16.5: The divine endowment is held to lead to liberation, the demonic to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava; you are born to the divine endowment.
16.6: There are two creations of beings in this world: the divine and the demonic.
The divine has been set out in detail; O Pārtha, hear about the demonic from me.
16.7: Demonic people know neither what to take up nor what to turn away from;
neither purity, nor even good conduct, nor truth is found in them.
16.8: They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord,
born of the union of man and woman; what else is its cause but desire?
16.9: Holding to this view, ruined in mind and of little understanding,
these men of cruel deeds rise up as enemies of the world, for its destruction.
16.10: Resorting to desire that can never be filled, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance,
having seized false notions through delusion, they act with impure vows.
16.11: Clinging to measureless anxiety that ends only with death,
holding the enjoyment of desires as the highest, sure that this is all,
16.12: bound by hundreds of nooses of hope, given over to desire and anger,
they strive by unjust means to amass wealth for the enjoyment of desires.
16.13: They think: This I have gained today; this wish I shall attain;
this wealth is mine, and this too will be mine in time.
16.14: That enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay the others too.
I am the master, I am the enjoyer; I am successful, mighty and happy.
16.15: I am wealthy and high-born; who else is there like me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice — thus deluded by ignorance,
16.16: their minds led astray by many thoughts, caught in the net of delusion,
attached to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
16.17: Self-conceited, unbending, filled with the pride and arrogance of wealth,
they offer sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy, not by the ordinance of scripture.
16.18: Given over to egoism, force, arrogance, desire and anger,
these envious men hate me, who dwell in their own bodies and in the bodies of others.
16.19: Those cruel men who hate me, the lowest of mankind, in the rounds of worldly existence
I hurl again and again, impure as they are, into demonic wombs alone.
16.20: Having entered demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth,
never reaching me, O son of Kuntī, they go from there to a state lower still.
16.21: This gate of hell, the ruin of the self, is threefold:
desire, anger and greed; therefore one should give up these three.
16.22: A man freed from these three gates to darkness, O son of Kuntī,
does what is good for himself, and so goes to the supreme state.
16.23: He who casts aside the ordinance of scripture and acts as his desires lead him
attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme state.
16.24: Therefore scripture is your authority in deciding what is to be done and what is not.
Knowing the action that the ordinance of scripture declares, you should perform it here.
16.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the sixteenth chapter, named Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga, the yoga of the division between the divine and the demonic endowments.
17.1: Those who set aside the ordinance of scripture and worship endowed with faith —
what is their standing, O Kṛṣṇa? Is it sattva, rajas or tamas: goodness, passion or darkness?
17.2: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature:
sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa. Hear about it.
17.3: The faith of each is in keeping with his inner being, O Bhārata.
A person is made of his faith: whatever his faith is, that indeed is he.
17.4: The sāttvika worship the gods; the rājasa worship the yakṣas and the rākṣasas;
the others, the tāmasa, worship the spirits of the dead and the hosts of ghosts.
17.5: Those people who practise a fierce austerity that scripture does not enjoin,
full of hypocrisy and egoism, and possessed of the force of desire and attachment,
17.6: who senselessly wear down the aggregate of elements in the body,
and me too, who dwell within the body: know them to be of demonic resolve.
17.7: The food that each holds dear is threefold too,
and so are sacrifice, austerity and giving. Hear how they differ.
17.8: Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness and delight,
that are savoury, rich, lasting and pleasing to the heart, are dear to the sāttvika.
17.9: Foods that are pungent, sour, salty, very hot, sharp, dry and burning
are liked by the rājasa; they bring pain, grief and disease.
17.10: Food that is half-cooked, has lost its taste, smells foul and has stood overnight,
and that is left over from a meal and impure, is dear to the tāmasa.
17.11: The sacrifice offered by those who do not crave its fruit, as the ordinance lays down,
with the mind settled in the thought that it simply ought to be offered, is sāttvika.
17.12: But the sacrifice made with its fruit in view, and also for show,
O best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be rājasa.
17.13: A sacrifice without ordinance, in which no food is given out, without mantras and without the priests' fee,
and devoid of faith, they call tāmasa.
17.14: Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness,
continence and non-violence: this is called austerity of the body.
17.15: Speech that causes no distress and is true, pleasant and beneficial,
and the regular recitation of the Veda: this is called austerity of speech.
17.16: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-control
and purity of intent: this is called austerity of the mind.
17.17: This threefold austerity, practised with supreme faith by men
who are steadfast and do not crave its fruit, they call sāttvika.
17.18: Austerity practised to win respect, honour and worship, and with hypocrisy too,
is declared here to be rājasa, unsteady and fleeting.
17.19: Austerity practised out of a deluded notion, by tormenting oneself,
or to bring ruin on another, is said to be tāmasa.
17.20: A gift given in the thought that it ought to be given, to one who does nothing in return,
at the right place and time and to a fit recipient: that gift is held to be sāttvika.
17.21: But a gift given to get a favour in return, or again with its fruit in view,
and given with vexation: that gift is held to be rājasa.
17.22: A gift given at the wrong place and time and to the unfit,
without respect and with contempt, is said to be tāmasa.
17.23: Om, tat, sat: this is held to be the threefold designation of Brahman, the Absolute.
By it, of old, the brāhmaṇas, the Vedas and the sacrifices were created.
17.24: Therefore the acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity of the expounders of Brahman,
laid down in the ordinances, always begin with the utterance of Om.
17.25: Uttering tat, with no thought of the fruit, the acts of sacrifice and austerity
and the many kinds of giving are performed by those who seek liberation.
17.26: Sat is the word used for what exists and for what is good;
and so, O Pārtha, an act worthy of praise is also called by the word sat.
17.27: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and giving is also called sat,
and any action done for their sake bears the name sat as well.
17.28: Whatever is offered in the fire, given, practised as austerity or done without faith
is called asat, O Pārtha; it is of no use either after death or here.
17.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the seventeenth chapter, named Śraddhātrayavibhāgayoga, the yoga of the threefold division of faith.
18.1: O mighty-armed one, I wish to know the truth of renunciation, saṃnyāsa,
and of relinquishment, tyāga, O Hṛṣīkeśa, each apart, O slayer of Keśin.
18.2: The sages know renunciation as the laying aside of actions done for desired ends;
the discerning call the giving up of the fruit of all actions relinquishment.
18.3: Some thinkers say that action is faulty and should be given up;
others say that acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be given up.
18.4: Hear my settled view on that relinquishment, O best of the Bharatas;
for relinquishment, O tiger among men, has been declared to be of three kinds.
18.5: Acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be given up; they must indeed be done.
Sacrifice, giving and austerity are what purify the wise.
18.6: But even these actions, giving up attachment and the fruits,
ought to be done: this, O Pārtha, is my settled and highest view.
18.7: But to renounce obligatory action is not proper;
abandoning it out of delusion is declared to be tāmasa.
18.8: He who gives up an action merely because it is painful, out of fear of bodily strain,
makes a rājasa relinquishment and does not gain the fruit of relinquishment at all.
18.9: When obligatory action is done simply because it ought to be done, O Arjuna,
giving up attachment and the fruit as well, that relinquishment is held to be sāttvika.
18.10: He does not hate inauspicious action, nor cling to auspicious action:
the relinquisher who is filled with sattva, wise, his doubts cut away.
18.11: For an embodied being cannot give up actions entirely;
but he who gives up the fruit of action is called a relinquisher.
18.12: The fruit of action is threefold: undesired, desired and mixed;
after death it comes to those who have not relinquished, but never to renouncers.
18.13: O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes,
declared in the Sāṅkhya, which brings actions to their end, for the accomplishment of all actions.
18.14: The seat (the body), likewise the doer, and the instruments of various kinds,
the many and distinct activities, and daiva, the divine, the fifth here.
18.15: Whatever action a man undertakes with body, speech and mind,
whether it is right or contrary to right, these five are its causes.
18.16: This being so, the man who sees the pure Self as the doer
sees so because his intellect is unformed; that man of poor understanding does not see.
18.17: He who has no ego of being the doer, and whose intellect is not tainted,
even though he slays these people, does not slay and is not bound.
18.18: Knowledge, the object of knowledge and the knower: these three are the impulse to action;
the instrument, the act and the doer: these three are what action rests on.
18.19: Knowledge, action and the doer are of three kinds only, by the difference of the guṇas, the three qualities of nature:
so the teaching that enumerates the guṇas declares; hear of these too as they are.
18.20: The knowledge by which one sees in all beings one imperishable reality,
undivided in the divided — know that knowledge to be sāttvika.
18.21: But the knowledge which, through separateness, perceives manifold entities of distinct kinds
in all beings — know that knowledge to be rājasa.
18.22: And that which clings to a single effect as though it were the whole, without reason,
without grasp of the truth, and petty — that is declared tāmasa.
18.23: The action that is prescribed, free from attachment, done without attraction or aversion,
by one who does not seek its fruit — that is called sāttvika.
18.24: But the action done by one who seeks to fulfil his desires, or again by one full of ego,
and performed with great toil — that is declared rājasa.
18.25: Without regard to the consequence, the loss, the harm to living beings and one's own capacity,
the action undertaken out of delusion — that is called tāmasa.
18.26: Free from attachment, not given to egoistic talk, endowed with steadiness and zeal,
unmoved in success and failure — such a doer is called sāttvika.
18.27: Full of attachment, eager for the fruit of action, greedy, harmful by nature, impure,
given to joy and sorrow — such a doer is declared rājasa.
18.28: Undisciplined, uncultured, unbending, deceitful, ruinous to others' livelihood, lazy,
despondent and procrastinating — such a doer is called tāmasa.
18.29: Hear the threefold distinction of the intellect and of steadiness, according to the guṇas,
as I set it out fully and one by one, O Dhanañjaya.
18.30: Engagement and withdrawal, what is to be done and what is not, fear and fearlessness,
bondage and liberation — the intellect that knows these, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
18.31: The intellect by which one knows dharma, what is right, and adharma, and what is to be done and what is not,
but not as they truly are — that intellect, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
18.32: The intellect which, enveloped in darkness, takes adharma to be dharma
and sees all things reversed — that intellect, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
18.33: The steadiness by which one holds in check the workings of the mind, the life-breath and the senses,
never wavering through yoga, the discipline of the mind — that steadiness, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
18.34: But the steadiness by which, O Arjuna, one holds fast to dharma, pleasure and wealth,
craving their fruit out of attachment — that steadiness, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
18.35: Sleep, fear, grief, despondency and arrogance:
the steadiness by which a dull-witted man does not give these up, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
18.36: And now hear from me, O best of the Bharatas, of the threefold happiness.
The happiness in which one delights through practice and reaches the end of sorrow,
18.37: that which is like poison at first but like nectar in the end,
born of the clarity of an intellect set on the Self — that happiness is declared sāttvika.
18.38: The happiness that comes from the contact of the senses with their objects, like nectar at first
but like poison in the end — that happiness is held to be rājasa.
18.39: The happiness that deludes oneself both at the start and in what follows,
arising from sleep, sloth and heedlessness — that is declared tāmasa.
18.40: There is nothing, on earth or again in heaven among the gods,
no being that could be free from these three guṇas born of prakṛti, primal nature.
18.41: O scorcher of foes, the duties of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, and those of śūdras,
are divided by the guṇas that arise from their own nature.
18.42: Calm, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance and uprightness,
knowledge, realised knowledge and faith are the duties of a brāhmaṇa, born of his nature.
18.43: Valour, vigour, steadiness, skill, and also not fleeing from battle,
generosity and lordliness are the duties of a kṣatriya, born of his nature.
18.44: Farming, cattle-rearing and trade are the duties of a vaiśya, born of his nature;
work that consists of service is likewise the duty of a śūdra, born of his nature.
18.45: Each man, devoted to his own duty, attains perfection.
Hear how one intent on his own duty finds perfection.
18.46: He from whom beings come forth and who pervades all this —
worshipping him with his own duty, a man attains perfection.
18.47: Better is one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well carried out.
Doing the work determined by his own nature, a man incurs no sin.
18.48: O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon the work one is born to, even if it has faults;
for all undertakings are covered by fault, as fire is by smoke.
18.49: He whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who has mastered himself and is free of craving,
attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of freedom from action.
18.50: How one who has reached perfection attains Brahman, the Absolute, learn from me
in brief, O son of Kuntī: it is the highest fulfilment of knowledge.
18.51: Endowed with a purified intellect, restraining himself with steadiness,
giving up sound and the other objects of sense, and casting off attraction and aversion,
18.52: resorting to solitude, eating little, with speech, body and mind held in check,
ever intent on the yoga of meditation, and firmly resting in dispassion,
18.53: having cast off egoism, strength, arrogance, desire, anger and possessions,
free from possessiveness and at peace, he is fit to become Brahman.
18.54: Having become Brahman, serene in mind, he neither grieves nor longs for anything;
the same towards all beings, he gains supreme devotion to me.
18.55: Through devotion he comes to know me truly, how great I am and who I am;
then, having known me truly, he enters into me at once.
18.56: One who takes refuge in me, even while always doing every kind of action,
reaches by my grace the eternal, imperishable state.
18.57: Consigning all actions to me in your mind, holding me as the highest,
resorting to the yoga of understanding, keep your mind on me at all times.
18.58: With your mind on me, you will pass over every difficulty by my grace;
but if out of egoism you will not hear me, you will perish.
18.59: If, relying on egoism, you think you will not fight,
this resolve of yours is false; your nature will drive you to it.
18.60: O son of Kuntī, bound by your own action, born of your nature,
what in your delusion you do not want to do, you will do even against your will.
18.61: The Lord abides in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna,
by his māyā, his power of illusion, turning all beings round as though they were mounted on a machine.
18.62: Go to him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by his grace you will reach supreme peace and the eternal abode.
18.63: Thus I have told you knowledge more secret than the secret itself.
Reflect on it fully, and do as you wish.
18.64: Hear once more my supreme word, the most secret of all.
You are dearly loved by me; for that reason I shall tell you what is for your good.
18.65: Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, bow down to me.
You will come to me alone; I make you a true promise, for you are dear to me.
18.66: Leaving all dharmas, all duties, aside, come to me alone for refuge.
I shall free you from all sins; do not grieve.
18.67: You should never speak this to one without austerity, nor to one without devotion,
nor to one who does not wish to hear, nor to one who finds fault with me.
18.68: He who will tell this supreme secret to my devotees,
having shown supreme devotion to me, will come to me alone, beyond doubt.
18.69: Among men there is none who does more to please me than he,
nor will there be another on earth more dear to me than he.
18.70: And he who will study this dialogue of ours, which accords with dharma,
by him I would be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge: such is my view.
18.71: The man who, full of faith and free from cavil, does no more than hear it,
he too, freed from sin, would reach the auspicious worlds of those whose deeds are holy.
18.72: O Pārtha, have you heard this with a one-pointed mind?
O Dhanañjaya, has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed?
18.73: My delusion is gone, and by your grace, O Acyuta, I have regained remembrance of my true self.
I stand firm, my doubts gone; I shall do as you say.
18.74: Thus I have heard this dialogue of Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha,
a wondrous dialogue that makes the hair stand on end.
18.75: By the grace of Vyāsa I have heard this supreme secret, this yoga,
directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, as he himself was declaring it.
18.76: O king, recalling over and over this wondrous, holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna,
I thrill with joy again and again.
18.77: And recalling over and over that most wondrous form of Hari,
O king, my amazement is great, and I thrill with joy again and again.
18.78: Where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, is, and where Pārtha the archer is,
there are fortune, victory, prosperity and firm, sound policy: this is my conviction.
18.iti: Om Tat Sat. Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eighteenth chapter, named Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga, the yoga of liberation through renunciation.

1.10: Aparyāpta and paryāpta can also mean unlimited and limited; the older commentators, Śrīdhara among them, read insufficient and sufficient, as here.
1.36: Ātatāyin, an aggressor: one who comes with weapon raised to kill, sets fire, gives poison, or seizes another's wealth, land or wife; the law-books allow such a one to be killed.
2.12: In Śaṅkara's reading the plural, we all, refers to the many bodies, not to many selves; Rāmānuja and Madhva read in it the eternal distinctness of the Lord and the many individual selves.
2.44: Śaṅkara takes samādhi here as the mind; others take it as meditative absorption: their resolute understanding does not become steady in samādhi.
2.46: This is Śaṅkara's reading; others read it as: a well is of as little use where water floods on every side as all the Vedas are to the brāhmaṇa who knows the truth.
2.53: Śaṅkara takes samādhi here as the Self, in which the mind is settled; others take it as meditative absorption.
3.9: Śaṅkara takes yajña here as the Lord, after the Veda's words yajño vai viṣṇuḥ; Rāmānuja takes it as the sacrifice and the other rites the scripture enjoins.
3.15: Rāmānuja reads Brahman here as the body, formed of prakṛti, and the Imperishable as the individual self.
3.41: Others read the verb as slay, as in the last verse of this chapter.
4.6: In Śaṅkara's reading, prakṛti here is the Lord's own māyā of the three guṇas, through which he is born only in seeming; Rāmānuja takes prakṛti as his own nature and ātmamāyā as his will.
4.21: Śaṅkara takes bodily action as action needed only to keep the body alive.
4.25: Śaṅkara takes yajña in the second line as the self: knowers of Brahman offer the self, as it appears with body and mind, by the self into Brahman, knowing it to be Brahman.
4.32: Brahman here is the Veda, in Śaṅkara's reading: these sacrifices are known through the Veda.
5.4: Sāṅkhya here is, in Śaṅkara's reading, the path of knowledge with the renunciation of action; Yoga is the yoga of action.
5.6: In Śaṅkara's reading Brahman here means renunciation itself, steadfastness in the knowledge of the Supreme; others take it as Brahman, the Absolute.
5.14: The master is, in Śaṅkara's reading, the Self, the embodied one of the verse before; nature is prakṛti, māyā. Others take the master as God.
6.7: Rāmānuja reads paramātmā as param ātmā: the self of such a one is perfectly composed.
6.44: Śaṅkara takes this to mean that he goes beyond the fruits of the rites the Veda enjoins.
6.46: Śaṅkara takes the men of knowledge here as those learned in the scriptures.
8.3: Rāmānuja takes the supreme Imperishable here as the individual self in its pure nature, freed from prakṛti, svabhāva as the matter joined to the self, and visarga as the union of man and woman that brings a body into being.
8.4: Śaṅkara takes Puruṣa here as Hiraṇyagarbha, the cosmic Person, who sustains the senses of all beings.
8.24: Śaṅkara takes fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the northern six months as the deities presiding over them, who lead the departed by the path of the gods (devayāna); the smoke and the rest of the next verse are the deities who lead by the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna).
In his reading, those who know Brahman here are its worshippers, who reach Brahman by stages.
8.25: In Śaṅkara's reading, the yogī here is one who performs the Vedic rites for their fruit.
9.32: Śaṅkara takes women, vaiśyas and śūdras as the instances of those of sinful birth; Śrīdhara and others count those of sinful birth as a separate group, as here.
10.6: Śaṅkara reads four with the Manus; Śrīdhara and others take the four of old as Sanaka and his three brothers, and the Manus as the fourteen.
10.34: Śaṅkara takes udbhava here as the rise, the prosperity, of those destined for it; Rāmānuja reads it as the birth of the beings that are yet to be.
11.39: Brahmā is called the grandfather of all beings; as his father, the Lord is the great-grandfather.
13.5: Śaṅkara takes brahmasūtrapada as the Upaniṣadic sentences that point to Brahman; Rāmānuja takes it as Bādarāyaṇa's Brahma-sūtras.
13.13: Śaṅkara reads anādimat paraṃ brahma, the beginningless supreme Brahman; Rāmānuja reads anādi matparaṃ brahma, the beginningless Brahman that has me as its highest.
14.2: Śaṅkara takes sādharmya as oneness with the Lord's own nature; Rāmānuja and Madhva take it as likeness to him in attributes.
15.16: Śaṅkara takes the imperishable here to be the Lord's power of māyā, the seed of the perishable world; Rāmānuja takes it to be the self freed from matter.
16.8: Śaṅkara reads aparasparasambhūtam as born of the union of man and woman; split as a-paraspara, it means that the world was not produced one thing from another, by any chain of causes.
17.10: Yātayāma is half-cooked with Śaṅkara; Rāmānuja and others take it as food kept too long, stale.
17.27: Śaṅkara takes tadarthīya, for their sake, as for the sake of sacrifice, giving and austerity, or for the sake of the Lord whom these three names denote.
18.10: Śaṅkara takes inauspicious action as action prompted by desire, which binds one to worldly existence, and auspicious action as obligatory action, which purifies the mind.
18.13: Śaṅkara takes Sāṅkhya here as the Vedānta, the teaching of the Self in which all actions come to an end; some commentators read kṛtānta as the settled doctrine.
18.14: Śaṅkara reads daiva as the deities who preside over the senses, as the sun over the eye; some take it as fate.
18.53: Following Śaṅkara, strength here is power joined with desire and attachment, not the body's natural strength, which cannot be given up.
18.66: Śaṅkara takes giving up all dharmas as the renunciation of all action; Rāmānuja takes it as giving up not the duties themselves but the sense of doership, ownership and fruit in them, holding the Lord alone as the means.
